member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Igi1.Cameras.Igi1HumanCamera
member.summary: Project I.G.I.'s HumanCamera orbit (camera/humancamera.c): mode 3, around a body on a ladder, a wire or another interaction, and mode 5, over the player's body once dead.

remarks.para: Both modes enter the same way (0x483360, 0x483D40): at no angle off the body's own frame, with the distance at 1024 and the target at 10240. The camera stands at the target distance behind the look point, along the orbit, and looks at it (0x4834D0's follow); the distance only eases toward the target, 341.33 a tick (0x483390). It is pulled in only where every one of eight points around the body is hidden from it (0x483A00): then 204.8 short of whatever the line from the look point met. A body seen from anywhere keeps the camera where it is.

Mode 5 also casts, each tick, four lines from the look point to the sides, top and bottom of a frame at the current distance (0x483EC0). A surface facing one pulls the camera to 1.05 times its depth along the orbit, never under a metre, distance and target both; with none struck the target grows 341.33 back toward 10240. The orbit's pitch is held within 75 degrees either way. The one-frame shot of the killer (0x4849B0) is left out: the mode's latch is cleared after its first frame (0x482700), so no player ever sees it.
The mouse turns the orbit with the player's own look settings, as every view of the remaster does; the look point and the distances move on the tick and are presented between their tick pair.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Igi1.GunShotTracerRenderer
member.summary: Draws the tracers the guns' GunShot tasks file, through the tracer shader: the original's thin amber line under the vanilla preset, the remaster's glowing streak under every other.

remarks.para: The retail line is the task's render, 0x47ABD0. Each live tracer is one pass of a round's march. Its two ends take the ammunition's colours at their distances along the round's range (), and their brightness is that same fraction, faded by the end's depth in view and floored at a fifth (). When both ends are on the same side of the eye the line goes through 0x4E0E20: clipped a tenth of a metre in front of the eye and submitted as a one-pixel line strip whose vertex alpha is the brightness, source-alpha blended, depth-tested without writing depth, and with Direct3D's fog switched off (0x50D4C0, 0x50DCC0, 0x50E000). The port draws it as a camera-facing strip wide in the image it is rasterised into. When the ends straddle the eye -- a round flying past the player -- 0x47C610 builds a world-space wedge instead: the two ends and a third point across, level, at alphas 0, one half and one half (a round from behind puts the third point at its start, at alpha 0). Drawing a tracer spends it: 0x47ABD0 zeroes its life and the task frees it on its next tick, so the port draws it every frame until then.

The remastered streak is a port addition, presentation only: the simulation files, spends and frees its tracers exactly as above whatever the preset. Each tracer this renderer has not seen before starts a streak of its own that flies from the start of its pass to its end at , a trail behind a hot head, so a round fired at the player is seen leaving the muzzle and coming in rather than flashing for one frame. It is light: the shader adds it in linear radiance at , which the bloom picks up.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Igi1.Igi1PresentationProvider.NightSkyLuminance
member.summary: The dome luminance at or under which a level is drawn as night.

remarks.para: Fitted to a gap in the data rather than to a continuum. Measured as over the thirteen missions that declare a sky, the daylit ones read 0.47 (1, 4), 0.50 (8), 0.52 (5) and 0.86 (2, 6, 10); the dark ones read 0.23 (12), 0.26 (11), 0.28 (3, 9), 0.30 (13) and 0.35 (7). Nothing falls between 0.35 and 0.47.

The dark six are what vanilla draws as night -- a slate or navy dome over ground lit by its bake -- and they are exactly the six the dynamic path drew as a bright noon, because their Dirlight is authored at the same 12 o'clock as everyone else's. Mission 14 is indoors and declares no sky.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Igi1.Igi1PresentationProvider.DaylightColour

member.remarks: The per-channel median of the Front Color over the seven daylit missions (1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10). A night level authors no day of its own, and its own sun cannot stand in: it is the light the original shines on unbaked models under that night sky, which the cycle uses as the moon.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Presentation.Igi1.Igi1PresentationProvider.NightExposureDrop
member.summary: How much exposure a night level takes off at full night, on top of the cycle's own.

remarks.para: Far less than the sequel's 0.632. That figure answers a sun left UP and painted nearly black, which the eye adaptation reads as a correctly exposed dark subject and lifts back to grey. These levels are lit by the cycle's own moon under the horizon-bound sun, so the lighting already computes their darkness and the adaptation meets a scene that is dark for the reason a real night is.

Measured on mission 3's ground from the spawn view, ultra against vanilla: 0.072 against 0.415 with the sequel's drop, 0.140 with this one and the brighter moon, sky and dark-adapted eye that came with it. The original lights its nights as a grey dusk; the remaster's is meant to read as night and still be playable, and this is where that was judged to sit.
Nothing for a daylit level, which keeps the sweep exactly as it was: the authored sun is a noon sun and the cycle's arc is fitted through it.

A level whose dome is painted as night is bound to the cycle by its NIGHT end, as the sequel's night levels are: it opens at midnight with its authored sun as the moon and its authored model ambient -- the GlobalLight band the original lights models with, equal to the Dirlight's back colour in every mission -- as the night fill, and the clock sweeps it up to a day it never authored. Its bakes are not whole, so the hybrid sun stays.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Igi1.World.HeldWeaponRenderer
member.summary: Draws the weapon the player is holding, at the bone the player's own rig puts it on.

remarks.para: This is the last link of a chain of three: the level declares a loadout, every WEAPON_ID_* resolves to a roster entry naming a Gun Model, and the model goes wherever the first-person rig's bone 3 is.

The original draws it the same way and in the same order — 0x4644A0 poses the view, draws 005_01_1, then asks the human for the weapon's transform (0x4600C0) and hands it to the weapon's own RigidDynCubeObj render (0x4A01B0). That render walks the object's child list, so a weapon is not necessarily one mesh: the Glock's body attaches a transient gun-flame effect, its slide and its magazine, while the MP5 attaches two further parts. Effect tasks are driven separately by the weapon state and are not rigid parts.

A child is not necessarily fixed to the body. Five of the part classes have a render handler that asks the human for an attachment of its own and replaces its transform with the answer, so the magazine rides bone 52 and the slide bone 55 while the body rides bone 3 — see . That is what animates a reload: those bones are moved by the reload clip independently of the one carrying the gun. Children that name no such class keep the position, orientation and material slots from the same magic-object tree used by placed world objects.

A caller that has no view rig to ask — a dropped pickup, a soldier's weapon, a missile — supplies no bone-driven attachments, and every part then falls back to its authored magic-object placement on the primary attachment. That is the whole difference between the two paths: retail gates the same three handlers on the first-person view being the one drawing (0x4E81F0 + 92).

It remains in the ordinary depth buffer, but not in the world's depth range. The retail view-model renderer (0x49F700) selects transform layer zero; 0x493580 gives it a 204.8-unit near plane instead of the world's 409.6. reproduces that 0.05 m foreground range, while starts the rig with fresh depth. The weapon therefore keeps normal arm-and-weapon self-occlusion without a close wall cutting through it. The physical wall pullback still determines where the model rests.

remarks.para: One textured quad per mark, facing along the struck surface's normal and sized by the material. Which texture and how big are not decided here — takes both out of the material the collision face names, because in the original the surface decides what a hit on it looks like and the bullet knows nothing about it.

The geometry streams through ONE fixed-capacity mesh whose vertices are replaced in place each frame (), with each texture's marks drawn as an index range of it. The original makes each mark a child of the struck object (0x47D380), drawn against its live transform — so a mark on a moving door moves with the door. member.summary: The smallest vertex capacity a page's mesh is created with.

remarks.para: Headroom, so that appending a chunk to a page does not recreate its mesh every time; the capacity doubles from here as the page fills, so a page reaching a thousand vertices is recreated four times over its whole life rather than once per chunk.

It is small because pages are: the batch key separates every level of detail, ground tile, layer slot and base-or-detail pass, and there are only so many chunks in a 2048 m cell that share all four. Measured over a level 1 panorama, the median page holds ELEVEN vertices and three quarters of them hold under twenty; the top percent reach a thousand or so. A floor of 4096 was charging 192 KB of device memory for a median page holding 528 bytes of geometry -- 2306 live pages, 105 412 vertices held against 9 445 376 allocated, some 486 MB of buffers for 5 MB of ground. The doubling is what handles the rare large page; the floor only has to cover the common tiny one.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Igi1.World.TerrainRenderer
member.summary: Draws a level's terrain: descends the octree from the camera, then draws each chunk the descent picked, uploading its geometry the first time it is needed.

remarks.para: Chunks are cached by position and level of detail rather than by octree record, because the octree is a DAG: one record is reused at several places and orientations, so its record index does not identify the geometry. The original caches on the same key, hashing the chunk's integer coordinates.

The ground texture is real data all the way down: the level's TextureModifier tasks pick a material per vertex through the terrain.bit masks, the material's band for the chunk's level of detail names a tile map, and the tile map indexes the level's terrain.tex. Where two materials meet, the second is blended over the first with the coverage in the vertex alpha.
Terrain culls back faces. The winding was settled by measurement: the .cmd triples are uniformly wound within every block, and only a mirrored orientation flips a chunk's facing.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Presentation.Igi1.World.TerrainShadowCaster
member.summary: The terrain as the ray-traced world should see it this frame: the chunks that were drawn, at the positions the vertex stage drew them, in a mesh of their own.

remarks.para: The batch pages the terrain is rasterised from are the wrong thing to trace. A page keeps every chunk ever streamed into it at its level of detail for as long as the cache retains it, the same ground is held again by the pages of the neighbouring levels, and the vertex stage slides each vertex towards where it sits at the next level by an amount that depends on the camera. A structure built over the pages therefore held two or three copies of every hill, none of them where the hill was on screen, and the sun's shadow rays hit the copies: the ground shadowed itself in sharp, chunk-shaped patches wherever a copy stood above the drawn surface.

So the caster is rebuilt from the descent. Every chunk it emits contributes its base layer, each vertex moved by the same morph the shader applies — the ramp on the target position, the Chebyshev distance from the camera, the offset and slope the terrain's fade window gives — so where it is on screen the caster is the drawn surface to the precision of a float. The descent is run without the frustum (see TerrainView.Panoramic): built from what was drawn, a hill behind the camera cast no shadow on the valley in front of it, and the valley went in and out of shadow as the player turned.

The mesh is a storage mesh whose buffers are written directly by the host, so it cannot be rewritten while a frame in flight is still building a structure over it. A small ring of meshes takes turns: a slot written now was last used frames ago, which is past the frames the device keeps in flight. A frame whose drawn set and camera are the last frame's resubmits the slot it has, and nothing is written or rebuilt.
